projects.title: Ignatius at Home
projects.tools: Python, FastAPI, Claude Code, Claude, ElevenLabs, Supabase, Render
projects.image_alt: A day of the retreat Come and See as a two-page spread: Duccio's Calling of Peter and Andrew on the left, and on the right the title Follow Me, Mark 1:16–20, the day's grace and the passage with a large first letter
projects.summary: I'm making the Spiritual Exercises this year in daily life, a retreat that arrives as weekly handout PDFs. This app turns material like that (a handout, a few passages, a photo of verses, or just an idea such as "the parables of Jesus, seven days") into a guided audio retreat prayed one day at a time. Each day follows lectio divina: the passage read four times, a reflection for the heart, a deep dive into the text's history and original language researched on the web, silence between two bells, and a painting to pray with. Around it: a spoken companion to talk the day over in real time, guided practices with timed silences and journaling, and an evening Examen that can be written around your own life. Built for 15-113, Effective Coding with AI, as the course's server-side project on Render.
projects.process: It was built spec first: a design spec and build plan before any code, then a spec-driven revision, a Clean Code cleanup, and a visual redesign from mockups, with every prompt logged. The judgements that mattered: the model plans the days and writes around the text, but never writes scripture, which is copied from the person's own material or fetched from the public-domain World English Bible; it is free for anyone, on an academic cloud's open models, free Microsoft voices and the free tiers of six search services, with Claude and ElevenLabs as the paid tier; the notes a person writes about themselves are hidden from anyone else, even in the build logs of the shared examples; and most of the late work was the iPhone, where a nested form blanked the whole app, a long label pushed the close button off the screen, and a guided session stalled whenever the screen turned off.

projects.title: Rink Rivals
projects.tools: Python, Flask, Claude Code, the NHL API, OpenAI
projects.image_alt: Rink Rivals comparing Sidney Crosby and Alex Ovechkin, with trophy badges and a season-by-season points chart
projects.summary: Type two NHL players and get their careers side by side: every regular-season statistic with the leader highlighted, each man's draft position and trophy case, and a season-by-season chart of their production. Then, if you want it settled, an LLM reads the whole comparison and declares a winner — it has to commit to a pick, defend it, and state the best argument against itself. Built for 15-113, Effective Coding with AI, as a study in what a small app owes the person reading it.
projects.process: The interesting work was refusing to do things. The NHL's search endpoint does not rank by relevance — "Marc-Andre Fleury" returns Marc-Andre Dorion first — so taking the first match silently renders the wrong career and never errors; a scoring function fixes it and a regression test asserts the endpoint still misbehaves. Skaters and goalies share almost no statistics, so the app declines to compare them rather than printing numbers that are true and meaningless. Shots against and games played measure workload, not quality, so they are shown but never scored, and longevity cannot masquerade as skill. The OpenAI key stays server-side: GitHub Pages has no server to hold a secret, and GitHub Secrets are build-time variables that would bake the key into the published JavaScript.

projects.title: Charlie Road
projects.image_alt: Charlie the cocker spaniel, in a sweater, hopping across a voxel road in Charlie Road
projects.summary: A browser replica of Crossy Road with Charlie, our nine-year-old cocker spaniel, in the chicken's place. It keeps the bones of the original (the voxel look, one hop per input, endless roads, rivers, and railways, a camera that punishes dawdling) and swaps in what matters to him: tennis balls instead of coins, a bark that stops traffic, squirrels to chase, his real outfits as unlocks, a giant caterpillar toy worth five balls, and a squirrel-piloted flying saucer where the eagle used to be.
projects.process: The first version came out of thirty minutes in class with Kiro: five iterations from colored rectangles to a fake-isometric board that never quite worked. The rebuild took an evening at home with Claude Code. I measured the camera angle from real gameplay screenshots, wrote a spec with machine-checkable acceptance criteria and fairness rules for the world generator, and let an autonomous run build it block by block, checking each block by stepping the simulation through a debug harness rather than trusting a screenshot. A second round after playing it added the bark, the saucer, combos, a daily challenge, and a shareable trading card. Every prompt, decision, and build step is in the repo.

projects.title: Can a computer pass an IQ test?
projects.image_alt: A 3x3 Raven's Progressive Matrices puzzle with the last cell missing and six answer options
projects.summary: Three programs, written eight years apart, sit the same 96 Raven's Progressive Matrices, the wordless reasoning test from 1936 that still turns up in hiring. A student's 2017 course project, run without changing a character, scores 34. A rule-based expert system I wrote this year with no language model, about 300 candidate if-then rules and a learned ranker, scores 59 in under a minute on a laptop. A current language model, sent the puzzle sheet and every cell as images, scores 93. Random guessing gets 13.
projects.process: Sixteen language models from nine companies ran the identical puzzles with the identical prompt, so the write-up can compare accuracy, cost, and speed side by side: four models tied at 92 while their prices differed almost five to one, five scored below the program with no AI in it, and one release changed how the model works at answer time and moved the score more than two years of scaling on either side. A neural network trained on thousands of invented puzzles scored 10, worse than guessing, and the reason why is the most useful lesson in the repo. Every number is generated from the raw results by a script, and every instruction that produced it is quoted in the prompt history.
